name: master-slave
context: Distributed computing systems where a designated master node coordinates work distribution, task scheduling, and result aggregation across a pool of worker slave nodes. The master owns the global state and decision-making; slaves execute tasks delegated to them and report results. This pattern is particularly suited to batch processing, parallel computation, and compute-intensive workloads where the work can be cleanly partitioned. While the terminology is contested in modern systems (leader-follower, primary-replica are common alternatives), the architectural shape — a coordinator plus workers — remains a fundamental tool for distributing computational work. The pattern scales horizontally by adding slave nodes, and the master can itself be replicated for high availability.
benefits: Simple coordination model: a single decision-maker eliminates conflicts and inconsistent scheduling choices
Horizontal scalability: adding slaves linearly increases throughput for partitionable workloads
Clear separation of concerns: master handles scheduling and fault management; slaves focus purely on task execution
Load balancing: master can route tasks to the least-loaded or most-capable slave
Fault tolerance through master replication: the master role can be replicated using consensus protocols for HA
Work isolation: slave failures are contained; the master reassigns a failed slave's work without disrupting other tasks
Deterministic task routing: tasks are processed in known order, simplifying debugging and reproducibility
tradeoffs: Master as bottleneck: a single master serializes scheduling decisions; at extreme scale, this becomes a throughput ceiling
Single point of failure: without master replication, master failure halts all processing
Network dependency for coordination: every task passes through the master for assignment and result collection
Slave resource heterogeneity: if slaves have different capabilities, naive load balancing leads to inefficiencies
Batch-oriented by nature: not well-suited to fine-grained, low-latency request-response workloads
Master knowledge of overall state: master must maintain sufficient state to make scheduling decisions, consuming memory
Network latency in task distribution: slaves may sit idle while waiting for the next task assignment over the network
use_cases: A distributed map-reduce job where a master node partitions a large dataset and assigns map tasks to worker nodes
A video encoding cluster where a master distributes encoding tasks to available slave nodes and aggregates completed files
A parallel database query engine where the coordinator parses queries and distributes execution fragments to worker processes
A build farm where a master node distributes compilation tasks across a pool of build agents
avoid_when: Sub-millisecond response times are required and task distribution latency is unacceptable
The workload is request-response rather than batch-oriented; the coordination overhead is disproportionate
Slaves are geographically distributed with high network latency between master and workers
The problem has no natural decomposition into independent tasks; subtasks have tight data dependencies
Maximum fault tolerance is required — master replication adds complexity that may exceed the SLA requirements
component_types: Master (Coordinator): Owns global task queue, scheduling policy, and result aggregation; makes all routing decisions
Slave (Worker): Executes assigned tasks; reports results or heartbeats back to the master; operates autonomously between assignments
Task Queue: The master draws from a queue of work units to distribute to slaves; can be centralized or partitioned
Heartbeat Monitor: Master tracks slave health through periodic heartbeats; detects failures and reassigns orphaned tasks
Result Aggregator: Collects and combines partial results from slaves into a final output
Scheduler: Policy engine deciding which slave receives which task; supports strategies like round-robin, least-loaded, or data-locality-aware
Failover Controller: Manages master replication and election when using consensus-based HA
anti_patterns: Master as Data Router: the master not only schedules but also passes large data through itself, becoming a bandwidth bottleneck
Stateless Slaves That Are Not: slaves maintaining hidden shared state, causing non-deterministic results when tasks collide
Fire-and-Forget Tasks: assigning tasks without result acknowledgment, leading to silent failures and incomplete computation
Unbounded Task Queues: task queue grows faster than slaves can consume it, leading to memory exhaustion and missed deadlines
Coarse-Grained Decomposition: defining too few large tasks that leave most slaves idle while a few slaves do all the work
Master Heartbeat as Single Point of Contention: excessive heartbeat frequency creates network overhead that degrades task throughput
design_principles: Idempotent Task Execution: tasks can be safely retried if a slave fails mid-execution; results are reproducible
Data Locality Awareness: schedule tasks on slaves that already hold the data they need, minimizing network transfer
Heartbeat-Based Failure Detection: detect slave failures within a bounded time window; too-aggressive heartbeats waste bandwidth
Master Replication for HA: use a consensus protocol so that master failure triggers automatic election of a new master without human intervention
Backpressure at the Task Queue: when all slaves are busy, the task queue must exert backpressure on producers to prevent unbounded growth
Task Result Durability: results should be written durably before the master is notified; slave crashes after computation but before reporting require recomputation handling
Graceful Degradation: when some slaves are slow or failed, return partial results if possible rather than failing the entire job
best_practices: Partition Work Evenly: measure task execution times and rebalance if variance is high; stragglers (slow slaves) can bottleneck the entire job
Separate Data from Computation: store data in a distributed filesystem (HDFS, S3) and schedule tasks where the data lives
Implement Speculative Execution: when a slave appears to be straggling, duplicate its task on another slave and take the first result
Make Tasks Coarse-Grained: amortize the coordination overhead of task assignment over meaningful computation; thousands of tiny tasks create coordination overhead
Persist Task State Outside the Master: store work queue and results in a durable external store so that master restart does not lose in-flight work
Use Leader Election for Master HA: ZooKeeper, etcd, or Consul can provide distributed consensus for master failover
Monitor Slave Utilization: track CPU, memory, and task completion rates per slave; an idle slave indicates a scheduling or data locality problem
